The study in one minute
The question was about the temple
Jesus had just said not one stone would be left on another. The disciples asked when, and what the sign would be.
The signs fit that generation
False messiahs, wars, famine, persecution and the gospel reaching the known world all appear in Acts and in Josephus before AD 70.
Flee Judea
The escape is local: from Judea to the mountains, before the winter, not on a Sabbath. Luke explains the sign as armies surrounding Jerusalem.
All these things would happen before Jesus’ hearers passed away. The other views read the phrase differently; the study weighs each.
Read it as the first hearers did
Who was speaking, to whom, where, and about what? Asked first, these questions point to the temple standing in front of them.
Every verse has a setting
Each verse is traced to the events of AD 30-73, with the evidence and the other readings beside it.
Cosmic words, historic judgement
Sun, moon and stars are the prophets’ language for the fall of nations, as with Babylon and Egypt.
Then the mission continues
After the old order fell, the task remains the same: make disciples of all nations.
An eyewitness of the war
Josephus was a Jewish commander who surrendered to Rome and wrote the history of the war he lived through.
He records a sword-shaped star, a voice in the temple and a gate that opened by itself, which the people misread.
A siege of unspeakable suffering
Famine, factions and fire: his account matches Jesus’ warnings closely, though his numbers should be read with care.
Read him well
Josephus wrote for Rome and for himself. He is a vital witness, not an infallible one.
Every age saw the signs
Wars, earthquakes and famines have been read as final signs in every century since the apostles.
Every date has passed
From the Montanists to modern prophecy books, every specific date set for the end has failed.
Jesus gave the signs a time
He said these things would come on his own generation, and told his hearers not to be alarmed.
Watch, but do not set dates
No one knows the day or the hour of the final coming; readiness is faithfulness, not calculation.
Two dates for one book
Revelation was written either in the 60s, before the temple fell, or around AD 95 under Domitian.
The book’s own clues
John measures a temple that is still standing, and the sixth king is reigning as he writes.
The early-church witness
The late date rests mainly on one sentence of Irenaeus, which can be read more than one way.
If Revelation was written before AD 70, its “soon” points first to the fall of Jerusalem.
Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel; the promise belongs to Abraham’s seed.
The Seed is Christ
Paul says the promise was to one Seed, Christ, and that all in him are heirs.
Gentiles are grafted into Israel’s tree; Jewish people can be grafted back in by faith.
Views differ fairly
Dispensational, covenantal and fulfilled readings are each set out in their own terms.
Three questions
When are believers gathered to Christ? What are the thousand years? Is the kingdom established at the return, or stewarded now?
The seven-year week
Pre-, mid- and post-tribulation views all assume a future seven-year period; amillennial and postmillennial views see no such week ahead.
The thousand years are read as the present reign of Christ, a coming golden age, or a reign on earth after his return.
Common ground
Every view confesses that Christ will come again, raise the dead and make all things new.
“Heaven and earth” in covenant language
Moses and the prophets called heaven and earth as witnesses, and used the words for Israel’s world and covenant.
The tabernacle as a small cosmos
Court, holy place and most holy place pictured land, sky and God’s throne.
A new creation begun
If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; Isaiah 65 is echoed in Revelation 21.
And completed at the end
Christians differ on how much is fulfilled now; all look for the renewal of all things.
Ask any question
Hundreds of questions on the end times, each with a short answer, a full answer, examples and the other views.
Reading keys first
Audience, time words, the Old Testament background and the New Testament’s own fulfilments guide every answer.
Learn from history
A graveyard of failed predictions and a wall of named “Antichrists” show why caution matters.
Search, then explore
Pick a topic, search a word, or let “Surprise me” choose a question.
The unveiling of Jesus Christ
Revelation is first a revelation of Christ: Lamb, Priest, King and Bridegroom.
Images with roots
Every image comes from the Old Testament, from the tabernacle to Eden.
The old and the new
The book moves from the old covenant city to the new Jerusalem, from the harlot to the bride.
A journey for every believer
Its call to overcome, to worship and to witness speaks to every generation.
Written to seven real churches
Revelation is a letter to churches in Asia Minor, about things that must soon take place.
A book of signs
God “signified” it: its images come from the prophets and must be read through them.
Sevens and more sevens
Seals, trumpets and bowls build in intensity, framed by the throne room and the Lamb.
Ten readings, one hope
Every view is read chapter by chapter, and all end with the Lamb on the throne and all things new.
